edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Μὴ ὑπονοείτω δέ τις ἡμᾶς ταῦτα λέγοντας ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων εἶναι τῶν λεγομένων μὲν Χριστιανῶν ἀθετούντων δὲ τὸ περὶ ἀναστάσεως κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς δόγμα. ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ τὸν οἱονεὶ ἀπὸ κόκκου „σίτου ἤ τινος τῶν λοιπῶν“ ἀνιστάμενον στάχυν ἢ δένδρον οὐδαμῶς παραστῆσαι ἔχουσιν. ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ ἀρέσκοντι ἑαυτῶν· ἡμεῖς δὲ πειθόμενοι ὅτι τὸ σπειρόμενον „οὐ ζωοποιεῖται, ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθάνῃ,“ “καὶ ὅτι „οὐ τὸ γενησόμενον σῶμα“ σπείρεται (ὁ γὰρ „θεὸς αὐτῷ δίδωσι σῶμα, καθὼς ἠθέλησε,“ μετὰ τὸ σπαρῆναι „ἐν φθορᾷ“ ἐγείρων αὐτὸ „ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ“ καὶ μετὰ τὸ σπαρῆναι „ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ“ ἐγείρων αὐτὸ „ἐν δόξῃ“ καὶ μετὰ τὸ σπαρῆναι „ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ“ ἐγείρων αὐτὸ „ἐν δυνάμει“ καὶ μετὰ τὸ σπαρῆναι „σῶμα ψυχικὸν“ ἐγείρων αὐτὸ „πνευματικὸν“), τηροῦμεν καὶ τὸ βούλημα τῆς ἐκκλησίας τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ τὸ μέγεθος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας τοῦ θεοῦ, παριστάντες αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ δυνατὸν οὐκ ἀποφάσει ἀλλὰ καὶ λόγῳ· εἰδότες ὅτι κἂν „οὐρανὸς καὶ γῆ“ παρέλθῃ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς, ἀλλ᾿ οἱ περὶ ἑκάστου „λόγοι“ ὄντες ὡς ἐν ὅλῳ μέρη ἢ ὡς ἐν γένει εἴδη τοῦ „ἐν ἀρχῇ“ λόγου „πρὸς τὸν θεὸν“ θεοῦ λόγου οὐδαμῶς παρελεύσονται. θέλομεν γὰρ ἀκούειν τοῦ εἰπόντος· „ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ παρελεύσεται, οἱ δὲ λόγοι μου οὐ μὴ παρέλθωσιν.“
thought_title: Words that will not pass away
pass_a_gloss: Let no one suspect (ὑπονοέω) that we, saying these things, are from those called Christians but setting aside (ἀθετέω) the doctrine about resurrection according to the Scriptures (γραφαί). For they are by no means (οὐδαμῶς) able to present (παρίστημι) the ear (στάχυς) or tree (δένδρον) rising as it were from a grain 'of wheat or of one of the rest', as far as concerns what pleases them (τὸ ἀρέσκον ἑαυτῶν = their own doctrine). But we, persuaded (πείθομαι) that what is sown 'is not made alive unless it dies', and that 'not the body that will be' is sown (for 'God gives it a body as he willed', after it is sown 'in corruption' raising it 'in incorruption', and after it is sown 'in dishonour' raising it 'in glory', and after it is sown 'in weakness' raising it 'in power', and after it is sown 'a soul-body' raising it 'spiritual'), keep (τηρέω) both the intention (βούλημα) of the church of Christ and the greatness (μέγεθος) of the promise (ἐπαγγελία) of God, presenting its possibility (τὸ δυνατόν) not by assertion (ἀπόφασις) but also by reason (λόγος); knowing that even if 'heaven and earth' pass away (παρέρχομαι) and the things in them, yet the 'words/principles' (λόγοι) concerning each thing, being as parts (μέρη) in a whole (ὅλον) or as species (εἴδη) in a genus (γένος) of the Word who was 'in the beginning' 'with God', God the Word (θεοῦ λόγου), will by no means pass away. For we wish (θέλω) to hear (ἀκούω) him who said: 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will by no means (οὐ μή) pass away.'

pass_b_english: Let no one suspect, when we say this, that we belong to those who are called Christians but reject the doctrine of the resurrection taught in the Scriptures. For on their own premises they have no way at all to show how a stalk or a tree rises, as it were, from a grain “of wheat or of some other kind” (1 Corinthians 15:37).

But we are persuaded that what is sown “is not made alive unless it dies” (1 Corinthians 15:36), and that what is sown is “not the body that is to be” (1 Corinthians 15:37); for “God gives it a body as he willed” (1 Corinthians 15:38), raising it “in incorruption” after it has been sown “in corruption,” raising it “in glory” after it has been sown “in dishonour,” raising it “in power” after it has been sown “in weakness,” and raising it “spiritual” after it has been sown “a natural body” (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). So we keep both the mind of the church of Christ and the greatness of God’s promise, and we show that it is possible, not by bare assertion but by argument as well. For we know that even if “heaven and earth” pass away, and the things in them, still the “words,” the principles of each thing, which stand to the Word who was “in the beginning” “with God,” God the Word (John 1:1), as parts to a whole or species to a genus, will never pass away. For we choose to listen to him who said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away” (Matthew 24:35; Mark 13:31; Luke 21:33).
notes: Origen plays on λόγοι: the rational principles of each thing and Christ's 'words' (Matthew 24:35); the English keeps 'words' in quotation marks and adds 'the principles of each thing' as an appositive to carry both senses, since a single English word cannot. θεοῦ λόγου after 'with God' echoes John 1:1 ('and the Word was God'), rendered 'God the Word'. The staged text has a full stop before ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ ἀρέσκοντι ἑαυτῶν, which belongs to the preceding clause ('on their own premises'); a stray opening quotation mark before καὶ ὅτι is ignored. οὐκ ἀποφάσει ἀλλὰ καὶ λόγῳ rendered 'not by bare assertion but by argument as well' (καί implies 'also'). 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away' matches Matthew 24:35 word for word; Mark 13:31 and Luke 21:33 are close parallels with small differences in wording; all three cited. The Christians who reject the resurrection are not named; Origen likely has in mind groups that denied any bodily resurrection.
